key_insight: Twisted, coherently bonded lithium niobate interfaces form nanoscale structural helices separated by screw dislocations, with torsional strain implying chiral dipolar helices rather than simple moiré patterns.
engineering_relevance: Coupled elastic deformation, dislocations, and ferroelectric polarization offer a route to chiral oxide interfaces and twistronics distinct from van der Waals stacks.
method: Map interface contrast using 4D-STEM and differential phase contrast imaging.
Model electron channeling along helical paths and directly image structural helices with electron ptychography.
Assess chirality using sample-inversion imaging and second-harmonic optical circular dichroism.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports directly imaged structural helices, unchanged DPC images after sample inversion, and unusually large interfacial optical circular-dichroism signals.
watch_item: Dipolar helices are inferred from strain and electromechanical coupling rather than directly imaged polarization, and the abstract provides no quantitative device-performance assessment.
